steps.narration: This is the part I care about most. At the end of the blue level, the tribes of the world have become nations, and here we open one of them, the United States, and look inside its economy. The logic is the same as everything you've just seen. In the biosphere, higher organisms live on the calories of the ones beneath them. In an economy, the top companies build their businesses on other businesses, on infrastructure, and on basic subsistence work, all standing on a foundational government. It's a food chain made of money.

The road of American lives since nineteen forty-six and the economy share a single time axis, so a year on the wave stands right beside the same year on the road. At the present moment, the cross-section of the road opens up into a wave. Each rib behind the crest is one year of the economy, and the wave widens as real output grows. The crest is the year you're looking at. One honest note before we go on: this is a model, built on public accounts plus my own assumptions, so treat it as a way of seeing, not a measurement.

Underneath the whole landscape is the bedrock: government. Every society has a different foundation, and in the United States it's a constitutional federal democracy. The pillars you see are sized by what the government spends: Social Security, health care, defense, schools, police, roads and courts, and interest to bondholders. Watch taxes fall into the bedrock from every household, and benefits rise back out of it to the people who receive them. Nothing on the hills above could stand without it.

On top of the bedrock, the economy is built in layers, each one standing on the ones beneath it. At the foot are raw materials and the basic infrastructure people need just to live. Above that, manufacturing and infrastructure. Then services, and at the top, technology. Each industry is a ridge, and its width is its share of the value the economy adds. The heights show an order of dependence, not importance. Just like the food chain, the top can't exist without everything underneath feeding it.

Companies live on these ridges the way people live on the road. There are seventy-five of them here. Each one is born on its industry's ridge, rises and falls with its market value, and then meets its fate. Some fail and fall to the ground. Some are bought and merge into their buyer. Some survive all the way to the crest. Their color tells you how they sell: gold for meeting real needs, rose for manufactured want, and ice for selling fear.

Follow a dollar to any market on these hills and watch it split. Wages run back down to the people who did the work. Taxes fall to the bedrock. And what's left over, the owners' surplus, climbs up as a gold river into a halo above the summit. Around the top firms you'll see rings of owners, the golden circles of people who hold the claims. Like the top of the food chain, they live on what flows up from everything below.

Now the people. On this landscape, class is altitude. Each group lives on the slope of whatever pays them, placed as close as possible to their source of value: the industry of their employer, the government, or family wealth. The out of work are on the valley floor. Working people climb the foothills and slopes, professionals and managers live higher up, and business owners sit just under the summits. The wealthiest, whose money is spread across everything, float above it all like clouds.

Money moves across the landscape in rivers of two colors. Rose is desire, and ice is fear, and between them they govern how people behave. Spending runs from households to each industry's market, colored by the motive behind it. Saving leaves over the crest into the future, as capital that builds what comes next. And debt arrives from the future: spending drawn from income people haven't earned yet. Watch where the rivers run, and you'll see what people want, and what they're afraid of.

Let's zoom all the way down to one person. Where they stand on this hillside is where they stand in the social market: which slope pays them, which rung they occupy, and who stands around them. In the universe graph, this person was one thin line inside a stream. Here, you can see the ground they're standing on. Keep in mind that they're synthetic, each one standing in for many real people, not anyone you could look up.

Now step inside that person's mind. There are five drives of desire and five drives of fear, and reason weighs them against each other to make a choice. Desire pulls toward the hills that pay and the things that please. Fear pushes away from debt, from loss, and from scarcity. Every river you saw on the landscape starts here, in decisions like this one, made over and over again. It's a simplified model of a mind, but the tug of war it shows is real.

People don't decide alone. Each encounter between two people is a prisoner's dilemma: both can cooperate, or either one can defect and try to take more. Over many rounds, one of the most successful strategies is called tit for tat. It opens kindly, then simply copies whatever its partner did last time. It retaliates when it's cheated, and it forgives as soon as the other side cooperates again. Here, the payoffs from all those encounters add up over time as wealth.

This is the ladder: one life's path across the landscape over time. Watch it climb and fall between the rungs. A new job can lift it, marriage can join two paths, children cost money and time, and debt can pull it down or help it climb. Beside it, you can compare where this person ended up with the rung their parents stood on. Anyone can move up or down this hillside. The real questions are how, and what it costs.

Groups play the same game as individuals. Companies, classes and whole tribes meet each other again and again, and each time they choose to cooperate or defect. You can watch cooperation, retaliation and forgiveness play out between them, and coalitions form wherever cooperating keeps paying off. It's the same logic that held the first human tribes together, now playing out on a landscape of money.

Let's pull back to the whole wave. This economy is the newest layer of the same chain of causes that started with the Big Bang: matter, then life, then people, and now the systems people build on top of each other. It's a model, with my assumptions built into it, and I hope you'll question them. But I built it because I think its shape is true. You are somewhere on this hillside, standing on everything beneath you, and moving with the wave into the future.
